answer.evidence: The tile is 48 px wide across all 32 rows and has no silhouette change. It is a stack of horizontal bands, each ending in a dark blue edge line at rows 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30. Each step has 2 rows of white tread, then either 2 more tread rows or 2 rows of pale-blue riser, then the line. Rows 3-4 and 8-9 are the only pale-blue strips, and each is only 2 rows tall. Rows 11-14, 21-24 and similar stretches are plain white, so no tall vertical south face is drawn. This matches stairs seen from above descending away from the viewer, where only treads show. It is a flat stepped surface with no standing front face of 3 or more rows, so it reads as top-down.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate reads as four stacked pale horizontal bands, closer to planks than to snow-cut stairs. Each tread has a light top, a white face and a thin blue-grey riser line, which gives about 4 lightness steps against 5-6 in the references. The measured facts look healthy (8 visible tones per tile, 0% near-flat, 0% neutral dark edges). By eye, though, the surface is smooth and gradient-like. It has no snow grain, no speckle, no per-step chipping and no side-wall or edge shading. The paving reference shades every stone individually and carries more texture. The candidate has no true dark outline, only tinted pale-blue riser lines, so it is not a sticker look. It still looks thinner and flatter than the references, and the stair structure (tread depth, cut sides) is weakly conveyed. When in doubt, fail.
